name: Majang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Joswig, Andreas. 2019. The Majang Language. PhD dissertation, Leiden University (LOT Dissertation Series 536). Utrecht/Amsterdam: LOT. 542 pp. Open full text:https://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/536_fulltext.pdf
catalog_locator: Part II, §II.3 'Distinctive Features' p.77; §II.6 'Tone' p.86; §II.7 'Word Structure' p.98; also Part I §I.11 'Typological Overview' p.48.
catalog_quote: p.77: "To be able to fully accommodate all phonological phenomena of Majang in a feature notation, three prosodic features would have to be introduced: [LONG], a tone and a register feature. But apart from the feature [LONG], prosodic features are not used in this language description." p.86: "Majang has two distinctive tone levels, which are called high and low (H and L). High tones can be both automatically and non-automatically downstepped in various situations (see section II.6.2). Falling and rising tones are created by combining high and low tones on the same syllable, which happens only at the end of a phonological word." p.98: "As already pointed out, the Majang language provides some clues about phonological word boundaries. The most important of these is the word-internal downstep rule which lowers the second of two adjacent underlying high tones within a word (see section II.6.2). ... Another tonal word-boundary marker is a contour tone, which can only appear on the final syllable of a phonological word." p.48: "The tonal inventory consists of two tones plus downstep (section II.6). ... Tone plays an extensive role, not only in distinguishing lexical items, but also in the grammar of Majang."
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Majang is described as a two-level tone language (H, L, downstep, word-final contours); the grammar's complete prosodic inventory is length, tone and register, with no stress or accent feature, and word demarcation is attributed to tonal cues rather than stress. No positive statement about where word stress falls exists in this or any other opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word defined tonally (word-internal downstep domain; contour tones only on word-final syllable). Getachew 2014 §4.3 p.70 independently: 'Majang is a tonal language that uses pitch (high and low tone) to distinguish words' -- also no stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Majang proper (maja1242, ISO mpe; Joswig's data mainly from Godare/Goji area speakers, Getachew's from Majangir Zone, Gambella). Cerulli 1948 'Masongo' = same language (older exonym).

sources.note: Nothing: the words 'stress'/'accent' never occur in a prosodic sense (a full-text search for stress/accent + reading of II.3-II.8). II.3 p.77 states the complete prosodic feature set needed for Majang is [LONG], tone and register; II.6 p.86ff two tone levels H/L with downstep, contour tones only word-finally; II.7 p.98 word boundaries cued by word-internal downstep and final contour tones; II.8 sentence tone. No word-stress/accent statement.
